title: The Rise and Fall of Homework
author: Aldeman, Chad
summary: Homework rates in American schools have undergone dramatic swings over the past four decades, and Chad Aldeman uses longitudinal NCES survey data to trace those swings and interrogate their implications for student achievement. Among 9-year-olds, the percentage reporting no homework fell sharply from 35% in 1984 to 18% by 2008 — and then reversed, rising back to 34% by the most recent data, while the percentage completing one-plus hours of homework per night also declined substantially. Thirteen-year-olds have followed a steadier but similarly downward trajectory. Aldeman connects these trends to a broader erosion of academic accountability: as states have weakened graduation standards, reduced school accountability requirements, and responded to equity critiques of homework, expectations on students have quietly collapsed. The troubling correlation is that homework levels and math achievement scores moved in parallel — rising together through the 1990s and falling together thereafter, with the steepest declines concentrated among the lowest achievers. While careful not to assert direct causation from correlational data, Aldeman argues that this parallel is hard to ignore and that the evidence supports some homework — particularly the reinforcement variety — as producing genuine learning gains and better habit formation. He points to modern digital platforms like ASSISTments, Zearn, and Khan Academy as examples of how homework can be redesigned for the current era rather than simply eliminated.
points: The percentage of 9-year-olds reporting no homework nearly doubled from 18% in 2008 to 34% recently — an extraordinary reversal that mirrors a broader weakening of academic accountability across states and districts.

The parallel between homework levels and math achievement scores is striking: both rose through the 1990s and early 2000s and then fell together after 2008, with the sharpest declines hitting lowest-achieving students hardest.

Equity critiques of homework — arguing that not all kids have the same at-home supports — have contributed to its decline, but the data suggest those critiques may have been applied too broadly, as the students most harmed by reduced homework are those same lower-achieving populations.

Modern homework doesn't have to look like the past: digital platforms like ASSISTments have RCT evidence of significant learning gains and solve for the immediate feedback and equity concerns that traditionally motivated homework elimination.

The ASSISTments program showed significant gains in research studies, suggesting that the problem is not homework per se but the design and targeting of homework — and that the window of contact with academic content represented by homework is a genuine opportunity that schools are currently wasting.
quotes: As math expert Tom Loveless has noted, the trends started to reverse in 2008. Since then, the percentage of 9-year-olds saying they had no homework surged from 18 to 34%. The percentage with less than an hour of work declined 14 points (60 to 46%).

It's hard to ignore the comparison between homework levels and achievement scores. As homework expectations ramped up throughout the 1990s and early 2000s, math achievement scores rose. Those increases were broadly shared across the performance spectrum — low achievers got better and so did higher achieving students.
But as homework demands started to drop off, so did student achievement scores. While fewer students were being given homework, the scores for the lowest achievers fell particularly fast.

Some advocates have argued that homework is inequitable because not all kids have the same at-home supports or responsibilities. However, it's hard to ignore the comparison between homework levels and achievement scores.

The ASSISTments program is a digital platform that lets teachers assign students math problems to work on at home, and it has built-in supports alongside immediate feedback and grading. Research studies have found it can lead to significant gains.
If the holy grail to learning is the amount of time students spend engaged, homework represents an opportunity for teachers to ask kids to squeeze in just a bit more practice time.

My suspicion is that it may be tied to broader cultural trends. States and school districts have cut back on accountability in a number of ways, from weakening graduation standards and easing back on school and district accountability requirements to limiting in-school suspensions and expulsions.
